target: AG1's claim that a national holiday would reduce or remove school/work schedule conflicts and thereby remove key scheduling barriers to voting.
objection: A federal Election Day holiday would not reliably solve the work-schedule problem for low-income workers, because private employers are not required to provide paid holiday time off and many retail/service workers may still have to work or lose wages to vote.

target: AG1's assumption that the holiday would be an effective turnout strategy on its own.
objection: An Election Day holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase turnout compared with other voting-access reforms, especially if the main scheduling barriers remain for the workers most affected.

target: AG1's broader proposal that Election Day should be a national holiday instead of using other reforms.
objection: State laws requiring employer time off for voting and automatic voter registration are more reliable, direct ways to improve turnout than making Election Day a federal holiday.

target: AG2's claim that a federal holiday would not reliably change private-sector work schedules for low-income workers.
objection: Many private employers reduce operations, close, or at least adjust schedules on federal holidays, so a national Election Day holiday would commonly change work schedules for many private-employer workers, including many low-income workers.

target: AG2's claim that low-income workers would face an unavoidable wage-loss tradeoff and thus the holiday would not help them.
objection: The feared wage-loss tradeoff is not an inherent result of a holiday, because many employers already provide time off or schedule adjustments on federal holidays, so the holiday would not predictably block schedule relief for many workers.

target: AG1's appeal to civic celebration and increased motivation as a reason for the holiday.
objection: Treating Election Day as a celebration may elevate civic participation in theory, but if low-income workers still cannot get time off, that motivation does not remove the practical barrier to voting.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday would increase turnout through civic engagement even if some scheduling barriers remain.
objection: Higher motivation or perceived civic value cannot be relied on to produce higher turnout when the underlying work-time constraints still prevent people from taking time to vote.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday would be justified because it elevates civic participation and democracy.
objection: If the holiday does not reliably remove the main barriers for low-income workers, then the civic-importance argument does not make it an effective turnout policy.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday would meaningfully improve access to voting by easing schedule conflicts.
objection: A holiday leaves voter-registration hurdles in place, because it does not automatically register eligible voters or change registration rules, so it cannot by itself provide comprehensive voting access.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday plus some schedule relief is enough to materially raise turnout.
objection: Even if a holiday helps some people with time off, unresolved registration barriers will still stop some eligible voters, so turnout gains cannot be substantial on that basis alone.

target: AG1's proposal that a holiday is preferable to targeted reforms.
objection: Targeted reforms such as employer time-off requirements and automatic voter registration directly address the key barriers to voting and are therefore better than relying on a federal holiday.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday is worse than targeted reforms because it does not solve voting access comprehensively.
objection: A national holiday can be implemented alongside other voting-access reforms rather than replacing them, so it is not inherently worse just because it is not a complete solution by itself.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday does not reliably produce meaningful turnout gains.
objection: A holiday can still produce real voting-access gains by removing a major barrier, even if it does not solve every voting obstacle at once.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday's turnout logic is invalid because it does not guarantee comprehensive access.
objection: The holiday can work as a complement to other reforms, combining practical access gains with civic symbolism, so it should not be rejected merely because it is not a substitute for every other reform.

target: AG1's argument that civic motivation and celebration will boost turnout.
objection: For many low-income workers, private retail and service employers can remain open and keep regular shifts on federal holidays, so the holiday does not reliably remove the work constraints that determine whether they can vote.

target: AG1's claim that increased motivation and civic value will translate into turnout.
objection: If practical work-time constraints remain, then motivation alone cannot be expected to overcome the inability to take time off to vote.

target: AG1's overall turnout rationale for a holiday.
objection: An Election Day holiday by itself is unlikely to produce meaningful turnout gains because it does not reliably solve the problems faced by low-income private-employer workers.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday would be a good reform because it combines motivation with access.
objection: Making Election Day a federal holiday disadvantages low-income workers because private employers are not required to provide paid time off, so workers may still have to work or lose wages to vote.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday meaningfully improves the ability to find time to vote.
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically register voters or fix registration requirements, so people blocked by registration problems still cannot vote even if schedules improve.

target: AG1's claim that easing schedules and boosting motivation together can reliably convert people into voters.
objection: If a voter is not registered or still faces registration hurdles, then better scheduling or higher motivation does not make that person able to cast a ballot.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday can add turnout gains on top of other reforms.
objection: The holiday is still not sufficient by itself to overcome major voting barriers, so targeted reforms remain the more reliable approach.

target: AG1's bottom-line proposal that Election Day should be a national holiday.
objection: Election Day should not be a national holiday because it leaves key work constraints in place for many low-income workers while also failing to address registration barriers.
